items.title: AI tools reduce friction in self-hosting by automating configuration and deployment, enabling more experimentation with technologies like NixOS and Debian-based systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI made self-hosting fun again
items.summary:
A long-time self-hosting enthusiast reports renewed excitement in managing personal infrastructure due to AI assistance. By leveraging AI coding agents to handle Docker Compose files, scripts, and configurations stored in Git repositories, the author finds it easier to try new services and automate updates, reducing the effort previously required for maintenance and experimentation.

The author highlights how AI has made it feasible to explore complex technologies such as NixOS and custom Debian-based boot images, tasks that previously seemed too time-consuming. Automation tools like Renovate and GitHub Actions streamline updates and deployments, allowing changes to be pushed or merged with minimal manual intervention. This integration of AI and automation has revitalized the author's self-hosting setup, including hardware upgrades and shifting services back to a more powerful home server.

items.title: Google requires AI agents to use Workspace MCP servers from February 2027, limiting Gmail API actions like sending email to partners only [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
items.summary:
Google announced that starting February 1, 2027, any AI-driven tool accessing Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and other Workspace services must use its MCP servers. The new policy restricts certain Gmail API functions such as sending, replying, or forwarding emails to partners with special access, while independent developers can only create drafts and label emails. This change affects AI assistants and tools built on Workspace APIs, requiring them to comply with new data processing and retention rules, including a 30-day cap on technical data retention and prohibitions on training AI models with Workspace data.

The MCP servers currently offer uneven API coverage, with Docs, Slides, and Tasks nearly complete but Gmail and Drive lacking key features needed for full workflow automation. Google has not clarified which partners qualify for extended Gmail capabilities or how it will enforce the new agent classification rules. Developers must self-declare AI agent use via OAuth client settings, and non-compliant tools risk access restrictions or account suspension. These changes aim to control AI access to Workspace data and ensure compliance with Google's terms of service.

items.title: Researchers propose a background independent algebraic quantization of vacuum general relativity using null cones, deriving finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and recovering black hole entropy corrections
items.originalTitle: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
items.summary:
Researchers propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes by solving gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones and promoting canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations. They construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation and obtain a Lorentzian path integral with absolutely convergent sums over intermediate states, computing finite graviton pair creation amplitudes nonperturbatively in Newton's constant.

Using diffeomorphism invariance, the team shows that macroscopic causal diamonds have finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and derives the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces, including logarithmic corrections for large Schwarzschild black holes consistent with previous Euclidean methods. They also derive the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low-energy limit of their theory, providing a new algebraic framework for quantum gravity.

items.title: Researchers develop method to certify proof depth in procedurally generated logic problems, identifying shortcut-free proofs and verifying problem difficulty across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
items.summary:
Researchers address the issue of overstated difficulty in procedurally generated logic problems by measuring the actual proof steps required relative to a set of inference rules. They compute the shortest proofs, indispensable premises, and export certificates verified by independent checkers to ensure accuracy in problem difficulty assessment.

The team audited eight datasets, finding variations in forced proof depth and shortcut presence, and constructed problems with proofs of specified structures using a catalog of shortcuts. Their approach includes fully checked problems with certificates, and training data mixing certified problem types showed better transfer performance for Qwen3 models across sizes from 0.6B to 8B parameters compared to previous derivation data.
items.description:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.

items.title: Researchers find vision and language AI models converge in Jacobian-space representations up to a rotation, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
items.summary:
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that AI models trained on different data modalities develop shared world representations. This study extends prior work by examining how vision and language models act on these internal representations, focusing on the Jacobian-space (J-space) vectors that influence model outputs. The researchers found that J-spaces of different models align approximately through a single rotation, which generalizes across words and classes not used in fitting.

Applying this rotation, a word vector from a language model can alter the object recognized by a vision-language model in an image region, change objects generated by an image generator, or raise class scores in an ImageNet classifier trained without text. These findings indicate that models not only represent the world similarly but also influence outputs in comparable ways, reinforcing the idea of convergent AI representations across modalities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

items.title: Researchers develop supervised learning confidence scores to gate large language model outputs, improving automation safety and accuracy on SQuAD and TruthfulQA datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
items.summary:
Researchers propose a supervised learning approach to generate reliable confidence scores for large language model (LLM) outputs, addressing the issue of LLMs producing incorrect answers with high confidence. They fit a linear confidence score head to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2-billion-parameter LLM backbone and train text-only metamodels for closed models, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain answers for human review. The confidence score head outperforms multiple baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets on datasets primarily composed of SQuAD and TruthfulQA answers.

The study finds that prompted confidence scores, while appearing well calibrated, lack the resolution needed for effective thresholding, and that the confidence score head remains the most robust method despite modest transferability to unseen datasets. This confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties such as safety or compliance, supporting more reliable deployment of AI decision-making systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce partial routing to delegate subtasks from expensive AI models to cheaper ones, improving task performance and reducing costs on ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
items.summary: Researchers propose partial routing, a method that enables a leading AI model to delegate suitable subtasks to a less costly worker model based on analysis of past task runs. This approach identifies recurring subtasks and measures each model's quality and cost, guiding delegation without retraining either model. Evaluations on ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 show that partial routing improves mean task performance and reduces costs compared to using the lead model alone or task-level routing. With a delegation parameter set to 0.75, the method increased the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 while lowering costs by 19%, and raised the Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. The study demonstrates that leveraging past execution data can enhance planning and delegation efficiency with minimal overhead.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.

items.title: Researchers propose CA-RAG, a retrieval-conditioning framework that integrates structural constraints and knowledge-graph relations to improve evidence selection for compliance-sensitive long-form generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
items.summary:
The paper introduces Constraint-Aligned Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CA-RAG), which enhances retrieval by incorporating ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations into section-specific queries. This approach aims to address limitations of standard retrieval methods that focus solely on semantic relevance and may omit mandatory information for compliance-sensitive documents. Evaluation shows CA-RAG improves precision, recall, and F1 scores over standard RAG at various retrieval budgets, particularly at k=6.

Generation experiments demonstrate that CA-RAG enhances compliance and reliability across multiple model and domain settings, outperforming generation-only constraint methods that achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results suggest that aligning retrieval with structural requirements can increase evidence sufficiency in long-form generation tasks requiring strict adherence to structural obligations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

items.title: Researchers introduce PeerReveal to detect fully AI-generated peer reviews across scientific domains, improving detection accuracy with adversarial training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PeerReveal, a new AI detector designed to distinguish fully AI-generated peer reviews from those partially rewritten by AI, across diverse scientific fields. The system bases its decisions on learned relationships between review claims and reference claims from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, supplemented by textual signals at the review level. PeerReveal was evaluated on PeerShift, a dataset of 5,430 reviews spanning machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, achieving a pooled Macro-F1 score of 70.52%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.48 points.

The team further enhanced PeerReveal's generalization through an adversarial training framework that uses a small local generator to produce challenging reviews, raising the pooled Macro-F1 score to 82.40%. These results indicate that incorporating richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more complex generation processes improves the robustness of AI-generated review detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33555v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.

items.title: Researchers introduce Aligned Machine, a public platform creating a Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark to evaluate semantic alignment in multimodal embedding models using human comparative judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
items.summary:
Aligned Machine is an interactive platform that gathers human comparative judgments to assess how well embedding models reflect human understanding of similarity across text and images. In an initial study with 115 participants labeling 2,875 pairs, the platform evaluated 12 popular embedding models and found only partial alignment with human judgments, with text-only models generally outperforming multimodal ones.

The platform uses a forced-choice task where participants select the more similar pair between two item pairs, enabling scalable, high-confidence data collection accessible to non-experts. Results showed multimodal model alignment varies by task type, being strongest for image-image comparisons and weakest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to grow with ongoing participation, supporting longitudinal studies, bias detection, and tracking concept drift in embedding models over time.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

items.title: Source-code audit and reanalysis of SkillsBench finds average skill lift of 18.7 percentage points with no statistically significant task-level reductions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does Skill Lift Actually Measure? A Source-Code-Level Audit and Noise-Aware Reanalysis of SkillsBench
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a source-code-level audit and noise-aware reanalysis of SkillsBench, a benchmark measuring agent skill improvements, analyzing 7,554 public trials across 1,421 configuration-task pairs. They identified grader dependence issues, placeholder skill directories, and additional built-in skills affecting results, with an overall average skill lift of 18.7 percentage points but no statistically significant reductions in task performance after correcting for multiple tests.

The audit revealed that observed negative differences in some tasks were likely due to run-sampling noise, as most cells lacked sufficient runs to detect decreases reliably. A gating strategy based on skill-free scores showed apparent improvements in logs but did not yield statistically significant gains on held-out data. The researchers have published their audit ledger and analysis scripts for transparency and further study.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33943v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.

A gating strategy based on skill-free scores showed apparent improvements in logs but did not yield statistically significant gains on held-out data. The researchers have published their audit ledger and analysis scripts for transparency and further study.

items.title: Researchers analyze six reasoning language models in auction bidding, identifying model and operator errors that reduce bid surplus by up to 17% on eBay and simulated markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Budget, Readout or Reasoning? Where Small Reasoning Models Lose Value in Auction Bidding
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated six open reasoning language models with 4 billion to 14 billion parameters on auction bidding tasks using win curves from eBay and a simulated advertising market called AuctionNet. They compared model-generated bids against an exact calculator and found that models often overlooked the best bid option despite ranking it highest internally, with errors biased toward higher bids rather than position in the list. These mistakes cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus achievable by the calculator under pay-your-bid pricing.

The study also identified losses due to operator choices, such as token limits truncating reasoning traces and premature answer requests before reasoning completion. Allowing models to finish reasoning improved performance significantly, with the weakest model's lead recovery doubling on both eBay and AuctionNet. An audit mechanism that flagged and corrected bids inconsistent with the model's own reasoning further increased the share of the calculator's lead recovered, demonstrating the importance of both model design and operational settings in auction bidding performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.

items.title: Researchers propose SOLO watermarking method for large language models to improve detection under repeated sampling by anchoring contexts on content via min-hash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SOLO: Towards Sample-Faithful and Detectable LLM Watermarking under Repeated Sampling via Content-Anchored Single-Owner Contexts
items.summary: Researchers introduce SOLO, a watermarking technique for large language models that maintains a request-scoped context history anchored on content selected by min-hash to reduce response coupling and improve watermark detection. SOLO aims to preserve self-consistency and uncertainty estimation while enabling each response to be independently detectable with a single key. Evaluations on five language models across three benchmarks show SOLO detects more watermarked responses at a 1% false positive rate than existing methods, even after random token edits, with code publicly available.
items.description: Researchers introduce SOLO, a watermarking technique for large language models that maintains a request-scoped context history anchored on content selected by min-hash to reduce response coupling and improve watermark detection. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34190v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Providers watermark the outputs of large language models, while applications sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, and uncertainty estimation. We show that deployed configurations of distortion-free watermarks, which deduplicate keyed contexts only within a response, couple the responses of a request: answer templates make all responses query the watermark with the same context before the answer, so collisions across responses, usually assumed rare, become the norm. Key pools reduce or avoid the coupling at the cost of multiple testing, and the exact remedy of a context history shared across the request leaves many positions unwatermarked. We propose SOLO, which keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so that siblings rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses, each detectable with a single key. On five language models from three families and three benchmarks, SOLO preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, also after randomly editing 10% of the tokens, and more than the context history on most clean tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhongliangGuo/solo-watermark.

items.title: MedSkill-E2 framework evaluates and improves autonomous skill use in medical AI agents, addressing skill Enable But Underuse with a new benchmark and evolution method [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce MedSkill-E2, a framework designed to evaluate and evolve skills used by large language model agents in medical tasks, focusing on the problem of skill Enable But Underuse (EBU) where agents fail to apply specified rules effectively during autonomous execution. They develop EBU-Bench, a benchmark covering 12 medical task groups, revealing a significant gap in skill-use accuracy between autonomous and guided use, averaging 43.94 percentage points across models and harnesses.

To address this, the team proposes EBU-Evolve, a method that refines skill instructions using feedback from both autonomous and guided executions, resulting in improvements of 33.33 to 55.17 percentage points in autonomous skill-use accuracy. These improvements persist across different models and harnesses, demonstrating that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies with execution context and that EBU can continue even after skills are accessed. The approach also enhances performance on unseen tasks within the same skill set, indicating potential for broader application in medical AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34250v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.

items.title: Researchers present vSFT framework for verbally supervised fine-tuning of language model agents at test time, improving success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
items.summary:
Researchers introduce verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT), a framework that enables large language model agents to receive dense natural language feedback and update their weights during test time. The system uses a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, where verbal supervision from failed trajectories is converted into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent.

The vSFT approach outperforms in-context learning and common reinforcement learning methods, with the Qwen3-4B model achieving higher success rates than GRPO and Reflexion by significant margins on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. The researchers suggest that learning how to adapt models dynamically at test time offers a promising direction for developing more capable self-improving agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

items.title: INSPIRE proposes two-stage reasoning framework for forecasting emerging entities in temporal knowledge graphs, improving Emerging MRR by up to 88.83% on ICEWS and GDELT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
items.summary:
INSPIRE introduces a two-stage forecasting approach to address challenges in temporal knowledge graphs where emerging entities have sparse and bursty interaction histories. The first stage learns a shared-pattern predictor with catalog-wide event memory, while the second stage optimizes an individual-evidence adapter combining semantic priors and long-range event statistics.

The framework applies coordinated masking and debiasing techniques to balance support and role supervision, improving ranking of unseen answers. Evaluations on four benchmarks show INSPIRE significantly outperforms existing methods, with the individual-evidence adapter further boosting performance metrics. The code for INSPIRE is publicly available for research use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.34708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

items.title: Study measures duration perception limits in 21 multimodal large language models using melody recognition against human baseline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated how 21 multimodal large language models perceive duration by testing their ability to recognize melodies slowed down at varying speeds, comparing results to human performance. Most models failed to recognize melodies without labeled in-context examples, while seven models performed reliably with such examples, generally matching median human recognition ranges. The study found that model recognition depends heavily on prompt design, with recognition peaks shifting based on example speed, prediction biases induced by melody titles, and accuracy declines at long note durations despite scientific pitch notation examples. Unlike humans, whose recognition windows are intrinsic, current models' temporal perception is largely shaped by the prompts provided.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.

items.title: Researchers find semantic density metrics do not predict task performance decline in LLM agent memory stores across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
items.summary:
A study analyzed 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods used by large language model (LLM) agents across diverse environments to determine if semantic density or related statistics could warn of impending task accuracy decline. The researchers found that mean pairwise cosine similarity and other geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics did not reliably predict early performance drops, with some local crowding measures only occasionally preceding decline but not outperforming simple stored-item counts.

Classifiers trained on this data and tested on extended PropWorld tasks frequently produced false alarms or missed actual declines, indicating that global semantic density is not a dependable indicator of memory collapse. The study also observed that size-limited memory stores remained stable over long task horizons, while failures occurred primarily when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded the model's input capacity, which was directly predicted by token growth.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.33184v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

items.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

items.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

items.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.

items.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.

items.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

items.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

items.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

items.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

items.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.

items.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

items.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
items.summary: arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

items.title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.

items.title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.

items.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

items.title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

items.originalTitle: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

items.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

items.title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

items.title: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.34756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.
